beginner.headline: Companies Try to Make Delivery Drones Quieter
beginner.brief: Some companies use drones, or flying machines, to bring orders to people's homes. These deliveries are becoming part of everyday life for many people in the US. Ashley Schmidt lives near Dallas and spends less time in her garden now. She does not like the noise from delivery drones above her home. She can hear them even inside her home. Companies are looking for ways to make drones quieter. Greenjets puts the parts that turn inside a cover to make less noise. Wing changes where its drones fly to avoid flying over the same homes again and again.

intermediate.headline: The Search for Quieter Delivery Drones
intermediate.brief: As drone deliveries become more common, manufacturers are looking for ways to reduce the sound their aircraft make. Ashley Schmidt now spends little time in her garden in North Garland, near Dallas. She cannot stand the sound of delivery drones flying overhead with her neighbours’ online orders. Steady traffic sounds may blend into the background, while the sudden sound of a drone can stand out. Researcher Antonio Torija Martinez says drone sounds can be particularly noticeable even when overall sound levels are relatively low. Drones operate at low altitudes, or heights, and may fly directly over residential areas, where people live. People who benefit from drone delivery services may be less bothered by their sound, according to Torija Martinez. London-based company Greenjets claims its system for powering drones can reduce their noise by at least two thirds. It places spinning blades inside a pod, a case that helps soften the sound and direct it away from the ground. It also slows the rotating blades and uses materials that reduce the sound caused by vibration, or repeated shaking. One propeller design has twisted, loop-shaped blades with no pointed tips. Amazon says its latest propellers produce almost half the perceived sound of its previous design, with a milder tone. Wing, which supplies drones for Walmart deliveries, varies its flight paths to avoid repeatedly flying over the same homes. Schmidt wants deliveries in her area to stop until the service no longer causes a nuisance, or an annoying problem.

advanced.headline: The Search for Quieter Delivery Drones
advanced.brief: For many people in the United States, delivery drones are ceasing to be a novelty and becoming part of everyday life. Ashley Schmidt, a resident of North Garland near Dallas, now spends little time in her garden. She attributes her discomfort to the sound of drones flying overhead with her neighbours' purchases. Whereas steady traffic may merge into the surrounding hum, a drone's sudden whine can cut through it. What Torija Martinez emphasises is that drone sound can be conspicuous even when overall sound levels are relatively low. He explains that communities with little previous exposure to aircraft noise may be especially sensitive to changes in their local soundscape, the combination of sounds around them. Research he cites suggests that reactions are stronger when a sound's source seems unfamiliar, intrusive or frequent, while people who benefit from drone services may be less troubled. He warns that currently localised complaints are likely to become more widespread as the sector expands. London-based Greenjets claims that its propulsion system, which generates the force to move a drone, can reduce drone noise by at least two thirds. Its design encloses spinning blades within a pod to muffle their sound and direct it away from the ground. The system also uses slower rotor speeds and materials that reduce sound caused by vibration. Greenjets' technology has helped conservationists in Africa seeking to monitor poachers from above without revealing their presence. For larger drones used in the Russia–Ukraine war, however, speed generally takes precedence over stealth, according to Tollast. Another propeller design features twisted, loop-shaped blades without pointed tips. Amazon says its latest drone designs use custom propellers that produce almost half the perceived sound of the previous generation, with a milder tone. Wing says that, alongside designing propellers to minimise sound, it varies flight paths to limit repeated overflights of individual homes or neighbourhoods. Schmidt would prefer deliveries in her area to stop until the service no longer causes a disturbance.
